questions.q: Which workload clearly favours a relational (SQL) database?
o: Money transfers needing multi-row transactions and strict constraints
Storing billions of independent sensor readings
Caching session tokens with automatic expiry
Storing large video files for streaming
questions.w: SQL offers ACID transactions, joins and constraints, which suits ledgers. Other stores suit other shapes of data.

questions.q: What best describes a document database such as MongoDB?
o: Self-contained JSON-like documents with a flexible schema
Fixed-width rows that are always held in rigid tables
Relationships stored as nodes and edges with properties
Plain key and value strings that are held only in memory
questions.w: Documents suit data that is read and written as a whole, such as a product or user profile with nested fields.

questions.q: Which store fits a very fast lookup of a value by key, such as a session or a rate-limit counter?
o: A key-value store such as Redis
A graph database
A column-family warehouse
A relational data mart
questions.w: Key-value stores give very low latency for simple access patterns but limited querying beyond the key.

questions.q: Which store fits finding friends-of-friends or detecting fraud rings?
o: A graph database such as Neo4j
A key-value store such as Redis
A document store such as MongoDB
A time-series database such as InfluxDB
questions.w: Traversing relationships is the core strength of graphs. In SQL such queries need many self-joins.

questions.q: Why do many NoSQL stores scale writes horizontally more easily?
o: They shard by key and give up cross-shard joins and transactions
They store far less data on each of the nodes in a cluster
They ignore durability entirely to gain more write speed
They keep only a single copy of the data to save disk space
questions.w: Partitioning by key spreads load across nodes. Queries must fit the partition key, so design the data model around access patterns.

questions.q: What is the main modelling difference between SQL and NoSQL?
o: SQL models data first, NoSQL often models around queries
SQL has no schema at all, while NoSQL always has a strict one
NoSQL is not able to store any relationships between records
NoSQL always enforces foreign keys between its collections
questions.w: In document and wide-column stores you often duplicate data to serve each read pattern efficiently, trading storage and update complexity.

questions.q: A team picks MongoDB just because it is "schema-less". What is the usual consequence?
o: The schema moves into application code, and messy data can build up
No schema ever needs to exist anywhere in the system again
The data becomes consistent automatically as time passes
Every query becomes faster without any extra design work
questions.w: Flexibility is helpful, but readers of the data still depend on its shape. Validate with schema rules and migrations.

Writing SQL in several languages
Replicating one database across many regions
Storing the same data in every database
questions.w: For example PostgreSQL for the ledger, Redis for sessions, Elasticsearch for search. The cost is more systems to operate and sync.
